items.excerpt: Anadolu’s recap of top stories from around the globe Seyit Samil Kurt 01 November 2026• Update: 01 November 2026 ISTANBUL Here's a rundown of all the news you need to start Sunday, including G20 foreign ministers concluding their Atlanta meeting with a focus on energy security, supply chains and geopolitical tensions; clashes during nationwide protests in France; the Yemeni army’s capture of a strategic mountain range from the Houthis; and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying he agreed with President Recep Tayyip Erdogan to work on establishing a new Black Sea grain corridor. G20 foreign ministers concluded two days of discussions in the US city of Atlanta focusing on energy security, global supply chain resilience and geopolitical tensions affecting international trade and economic stability, according to a statement by the US presidency. The meeting, held Oct. 30 - 31 during the 250th anniversary year of US independence, was part of Washington's effort to refocus the G20 on its core mission of addressing global economic challenges and promoting prosperity. In the chair's statement, the US presidency said the foreign ministers held "candid discussions" on Washington's priorities, including disruptions affecting strategic maritime routes such as the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Energy security emerged as a central theme, with the statement emphasizing the importance of affordable, abundant, and reliable energy supplies for economic growth and improved living standards. - Clashes reported in several French cities during nationwide protests Clashes between protesters and police were reported in several French cities during nationwide demonstrations, with police using tear gas in Lyon and Grenoble, as 15,000 people took part in 65 actions in France, according to media reports. In Lyon, tensions emerged after some demonstrators tried to leave the authorized route and move toward the city center near Place Jean Mace, prompting police to use tear gas, broadcaster France info reported. In Grenoble, southeastern France, police also used tear gas after initial tensions near Place Gustave Rivet, where a march was split into two. In the port city of Marseille, clashes broke out at the front of an unauthorized march, with protesters throwing paving stones at riot police blocking Boulevard Chave. Officers responded by charging the crowd, while the march continued toward Saint-Charles train station. Scuffles between protesters and police were also reported in Toulouse, Rennes, and Nantes. - Yemeni army captures strategic mountain range from Houthis in Al-Jawf The Yemeni army has completed its capture of a strategic mountain range in the northern province of Al-Jawf following battles with Houthi forces, according to a field commander. Col. Rabie al-Qurashi, an army field commander in Al-Jawf, told Anadolu that government forces secured the entire Huwayshian mountain range east of Al-Hazm, the provincial capital. He said the advance followed fighting with the Houthis and was backed by warplanes that destroyed dozens of vehicles belonging to the group. The military operation remains underway, he added. The mountains form the first line of defense for Al-Hazm, which remains under Houthi control, said al-Qurashi. - Zelenskyy says he agreed with President Erdogan to work on establishing new Black Sea grain corridor Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he had agreed with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan to work on establishing a new Black Sea grain corridor. “Today, I reached an agreement with President Erdogan to work on the Black Sea grain corridor,” he said during a joint news conference in Istanbul, following talks with Erdogan. Zelenskyy said Türkiye supports efforts to ensure safe navigation in the Black Sea and restore normal living conditions. ... - Golden State Valkyries beat Atlanta Dream to win first WNBA championship The Golden State Valkyries defeated the Atlanta Dream 68-63 to win their first Women's National Basketball Association (WNBA) championship in their second season. French international Gabby Williams led Golden State with 30 points in the decisive Game 7 at Chase Center in San Francisco, helping the team secure a 4-3 victory in the best-of-seven Finals series. Williams scored 28 of her points in the second half, including a crucial 3-pointer with just over two minutes remaining that put Golden State ahead for good. Atlanta led 30-24 at halftime, but the Valkyries rallied in the third quarter, outscoring the Dream 21-14 to take a narrow lead into the final period. Kiah Stokes contributed 13 rebounds for Golden State, while Veronica Burton made two late free throws to seal the victory. The game marked the first Game 7 in WNBA Finals history, with the championship series expanded to a best-of-seven format in 2025.

items.excerpt: Iran says no plans to meet U.S. officials, consultations with mediators continue Iranian Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi said that Tehran currently has no plans to meet with U.S. officials, while consultations with Qatari and Pakistani mediators continue over Iran's conditions for resolving the crisis, Qatar's Al Jazeera reported Saturday. In an interview with Al Jazeera, Araghchi dismissed reports of possible meetings as media speculation, saying Iran saw no need to meet with American officials at present. He said Tehran would decide whether to hold direct or indirect negotiations after Washington accepted Iran's conditions. G20 FM meeting ends without joint communique amid deep divisions A two-day meeting of Group of 20 (G20) foreign ministers ended here Saturday without a joint communique, as participants failed to reach consensus on major global geopolitical and economic security issues amid the Ukraine crisis and the U.S.-Iran conflict. Chaired by U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the meeting addressed geopolitical tensions, energy security and supply chains. At a closing news conference, Rubio highlighted freedom of navigation in key waterways, including the Strait of Hormuz and the Black Sea, along with critical mineral supply chains and food security. He said participants recognized the importance of these issues but remained divided over their solutions. ... Around 320,000 people take part in protests across France: media Around 320,000 people took part in a new round of protests across France on Saturday, according to French daily Le Monde which cited figures from the Interior Ministry. In Paris, the Interior Ministry put the number of demonstrators at 70,000 as of 5 p.m. local time (1600 GMT). However, youth unions and associations representing high school and university students put the nationwide turnout at nearly 500,000, including 200,000 in Paris. The protests disrupted public transport. Paris public transport operator RATP announced on its website that more than 40 metro stations had been closed on Saturday. ... In Paris, clashes broke out near Porte de Charenton, the authorized endpoint of the march, with protesters throwing projectiles at police who responded with tear gas, Le Monde reported.

items.title: US jobs pickup may keep Federal Reserve on track to hike rates again | World News - Business Standard
items.excerpt: 8 min read Last Updated : Nov 01 2026 | 8:47 AM IST By Matthew Boesler and Craig Stirling Jobs week lies ahead for the US, which means a heavy slate of data ahead of the capstone monthly employment report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics on Friday. Forecasters expect the report to show monthly job growth more than doubled in October, to 65,000, while the unemployment rate remained steady at 4.2%. That would leave the Federal Reserve on track for additional interest-rate increases in the months ahead to combat inflation. Other labor-market data in the coming week could reinforce the stability theme. A monthly report on job openings due on Tuesday is expected to show listings ticked higher in September, and economists will also scrutinize numbers on layoffs and quitting. Weekly jobless claims figures out Thursday, meanwhile, are seen remaining near the lowest levels in decades.

items.title: Mixed economic forecast weighs heavy ahead of midterms : NPR - Bytes Europe
items.excerpt: November 1, 2026 There was a mixed Halloween bag of economic news this week. GDP growth is up, but so are prices. For now at least, interest rates are staying the same. What does that mean for the midterm elections? SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST: As we just heard, many midterm races are extremely tight. And for voters, the economy has consistently ranked as a top issue driving them to the polls. This week, just days away from Election Day, we got some key economic news. New GDP numbers show the U.S. economy is growing at a healthy clip, but inflation remains stubbornly high. The Federal Reserve met and decided not to raise interest rates, but higher borrowing costs could still be in store by the end of the year. So what does that mean for the midterms? NPR’s Scott Horsley is with us to explain. SCOTT HORSLEY, BYLINE: Hi. Good to be with you. PFEIFFER: So affordability, that word we hear over and over and over again. It’s at the top of mind of so many voters. What is the new economic data tell us about that? HORSLEY: Well, it tells us affordability is still a challenge. You know, the cost of living keeps going up, and people’s paychecks are not keeping pace. This week, the Commerce Department clocked inflation in September at 3.6%. That’s higher than the month before. And significantly, it’s higher than it was when President Trump returned to the White House. That’s a big reason nearly two-thirds of Americans disapprove of the president’s economic stewardship. Voters punished Democrats for inflation back in 2024, and they may decide to punish Republicans this time around. PFEIFFER: Yet we have the seeming contradiction, which is that the latest numbers show the economy is growing. So why isn’t that registering or paying off for ordinary voters? HORSLEY: Yeah. The economy did perk up a bit in late summer and early fall. GDP, which is the broadest measure of economic activity, grew at an annual rate of 3.4% in July, August and September. That’s up from 2.2% the previous quarter. Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said this past week, that’s a good sign. KEVIN WARSH: The economy is strong. The economy is pointing in the right direction. HORSLEY: But a lot of that GDP growth is being driven by the huge investment in artificial intelligence. And, you know, if you build data centers for a living, you’re pretty busy these days. But otherwise, this burst of economic growth has not been accompanied by a burst of new jobs. PFEIFFER: And, Scott, what about the job market? What about unemployment numbers? HORSLEY: Yeah, the job market is still really sluggish. Employers added just 29,000 jobs in September. We’re going to get the October numbers this coming week. Even though unemployment is low, just 4.2%, most people don’t feel confident that if they quit their job, they can find another one. So they’re just staying put. And Chief Economist Mark Zandi of Moody’s Analytics, says that means there’s not much pressure on employers to raise wages. MARK ZANDI: There’s no hiring. Hiring rates are extraordinarily low, and that’s just not consistent with a healthy labor market. HORSLEY: Wages are growing more slowly than they used to. New figures for September show spending rose 2.5 times as fast as wages did. So it’s no wonder people feel concerned about affordability. PFEIFFER: And we know that many people are aggravated about everyday purchases, like gasoline and groceries. But then there are the major purchases, like a house, which is usually what makes people feel economically secure. How is the housing market look in terms of the ability to buy one? HORSLEY: I’m afraid the housing market is still haunted by high mortgage rates. Even though the Fed did not raise short-term borrowing costs this week, longer term rates are still high. The average cost of a 30 year home loan is around 7.25%. And Zandi says that’s keeping a lot of would-be buyers on the sidelines. ZANDI: I had been hopeful before this run up in rates that mortgage rates would hang around 6%. And if that were the case, then the housing market would start to fall. We get more home sales. But no, we’re now well north of 7% on a fixed rate mortgage. Housing is the most interest rate sensitive sector of the economy, and it is taking it on the chin. HORSLEY: The housing component of GDP has actually been negative in 8 of the last 10 quarters.

items.title: Speech by Vice Chair Jefferson on the U.S. economy and monetary policy - Federal Reserve Board
items.excerpt: October 01, 2026 ### The U.S. ... While I view the risks to both economic activity and employment as ... Inflation Turning to the price-stability side of our mandate, I will start by acknowledging that inflation has been too high for too long. The 12-month change in the personal consumption expenditures price index, the blue line in figure 6, was 3.4 percent in August. While inflation has eased from pandemic highs, it has remained above our 2 percent target for more than five years. The 12-month change in core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, the dashed red line, was somewhat milder. The predominant factor driving the recent pickup in headline inflation is energy prices, including gasoline and diesel costs. Oil prices have been quite volatile, and global energy supplies have come under renewed strain, reflecting heightened geopolitical tensions. I remain concerned about the risk of higher energy prices leading to a persistent rise in inflation more broadly. ... Survey-based short-term measures of inflation expectations are elevated. Most measures of longer-term inflation expectations, however, have remained stable at levels consistent with 2 percent inflation. These developments suggest that we are not yet seeing spillovers from tariffs, energy price shocks, and the surge in certain categories of goods prices into broader and more persistent inflation. But if actual inflation remains above our target, then households and businesses may eventually stop believing that we will return inflation to 2 percent. This potential uncertainty could lead to a rise in longer-term inflation expectations and affect wage- and price-setting decisions, and I am committed to avoiding this outcome. As my base case, I expect inflation to be elevated in the short run before resuming its decline toward our 2 percent goal as the effects of energy and other price shocks fade. I view risks to my inflation forecast as tilted to the upside due to recent geopolitical developments and stronger-than-anticipated aggregate demand.

items.title: US midterms enter final weekend as Alaska, California ballot fights heat up | World News - Business Standard
items.excerpt: 5 min read Last Updated : Nov 01 2026 | 8:22 AM IST ... President Donald Trump's administration pressed a criminal investigation into Alaska's pivotal US Senate race and said on Saturday it would likely take its fight over thousands of California mail-in ballots to the Supreme Court, as the midterm campaign for control of Congress entered its final weekend. In Alaska, federal prosecutors are investigating whether aides to Democratic challenger Mary Peltola helped to recruit a retired schoolteacher, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., to run because his name is similar to the Republican incumbent, Senator Dan S. Sullivan. The closely contested race is seen as crucial to Democrats' hopes of taking the Senate in Tuesday's vote. It is one of 35 Senate races, along with all 435 House seats, that will ‌decide whether Trump's Republicans keep control of Congress for his final two years in office. Republicans hold a ​53-47 Senate majority and a narrow edge in the House. Early voting has set a ​record. More than 51 million Americans have already cast ballots in person or by mail, according to the University of Florida's Election Lab, up from nearly 46 million who voted before Election Day at ​the last midterms in 2022. ## US appeals court rejects Trump's bid to set aside 20,000 California votes In California, a federal appeals court this week ruled 2-1 that the Justice Department had failed to justify its emergency bid to force the state to set aside mail ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters it alleges are likely noncitizens. "I hesitate to give a final answer, but I think probably the Supreme Court's next on this one," acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter told Fox News on Saturday, adding that any request for Supreme Court consideration would come before Tuesday's election. Trump has been on a campaign blitz in multiple states over the past month but is spending Saturday at his Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida. ​He returns to the campaign trail on Sunday in Kansas and Iowa. ### ALASKA PROBE INTENSIFIES The Justice Department's top prosecutor in Alaska, US Attorney Michael Heyman, said at a Friday press conference that a recent New York Times article, saying there ‌had been an effort to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. had driven a "surge" of FBI resources onto the case. Heyman said he had assigned several prosecutors to it and that investigative steps were ​taking place "intensely and swiftly." Peltola and the campaign committee have denied involvement in any effort to recruit the second Sullivan. The retired teacher has denied coordinating with Peltola's campaign. Voters in Alaska have largely dismissed the fight over the ballot. "I knew which Dan Sullivan was which Dan Sullivan, you know? It's very clear on the ballot," Anchorage resident Mickey Buster, 36, said as he stood outside a polling place on Saturday. But another Anchorage voter, Carol Riggs, 52, said she was disappointed by the entire situation ‌and the possibility it "muddies the water for some voters, potentially." ### MICHIGAN RIFT In Michigan, where ​Democrat Abdul El-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers in another closely watched Senate race, El-Sayed's feud with the ‌rival he beat in the primary, US Representative Haley Stevens, flared again. El-Sayed's campaign asked Stevens to skip his events through Election Day so as "not to distract from the central issues of the campaign," a ‌person familiar with the matter said. Stevens has backed El-Sayed but demanded he condemn an outside group's ad blaming Israel for high grocery prices and apologize for past rhetoric about Israel. "It's certainly unhelpful to the El-Sayed ​campaign to have continued visible division within the party just before Election Day," said Matt Grossmann, a political scientist at Michigan State University. Polls show El-Sayed has largely consolidated Democratic support. ### TRUMP'S PRESSURE CAMPAIGN ON STATES The administration, beyond its bid to block the counting of ballots from more than 20,000 California voters it alleges could be noncitizens, ​has sued roughly 30 states and the District of Columbia seeking unredacted voter rolls. The legal maneuvers have alarmed state election officials. Under the Constitution, states have primary authority over how elections are run. On Friday, a federal judge ordered the Justice Department to stop threatening to prosecute California election officials who defy its directives. California Governor Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, on Saturday warned the ‌state's top federal judges that the Justice Department may seek warrants to seize ballots before results are certified, though he said he did not know of any pending request. Newsom said in a letter to the judges ‌that the only reason to seize ballots "would be to interfere" in the count. Sean Morales-Doyle of the Brennan Center for Justice said the efforts, while unlikely to win in court, aim at "creating uncertainty, sowing fear, distrust, chaos," in hopes of pressuring officials such as Alaska's lieutenant governor "to do something that they're not supposed to do." Even so, 76% of US voters are confident their ballots will be counted accurately, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted from September 30 to October 5, with confidence about equally high among Republicans and Democrats.

items.excerpt: Author: Associated Press Published: 12:00 AM EDT November 1, 2026 Updated: 12:04 AM EDT November 1, 2026 Iran targeted US air defenses then hit aircraft and buildings on Mideast bases, AP analysis finds WASHINGTON (AP) — Iran's strikes on more than two dozen U.S. bases in the Middle East focused on early-warning systems before hitting aircraft and buildings, causing billions of dollars in equipment damage, according to an Associated Press analysis. The AP independently verified damage to American targets using satellite imagery from multiple providers and spoke to four regional officials who were briefed or have firsthand knowledge of what was hit. The AP found that, through August, more than 115 drone or missile strikes claimed by Iran or Iranian-backed militias damaged or destroyed structures on 26 military bases and other sites with U.S. equipment. The AP found that Iran initially focused its attacks on aircraft hangars and systems that detect incoming strikes, clearing the way for further strikes on warehouses, troop housing and more. The damage has significantly reshaped the American foothold in the Middle East, with two regional officials saying the U.S. has moved many of its assets out of the Persian Gulf. That includes aircraft, air defense systems, communications systems and other equipment crucial to base operations, one of those officials said. The impact of the damage raises questions about American defenses in the region as President Donald Trump considers new strikes after Tuesday's midterm elections and Tehran has vowed major retaliation. A return to hostilities threatens additional costly damage to bases, which would heighten uncertainty about whether the United States will choose to rebuild its bases and equipment in the region when the war ends. 'Grasping at straws': Judge dismisses Trump suit against Wall Street Journal over Epstein letter Saying the president was “grasping at straws,” a federal judge on Saturday threw out Donald Trump’s $10 billion lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal and media mogul Rupert Murdoch over a story reporting on his ties to Jeffrey Epstein. U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles in Miami dismissed the suit with prejudice, ruling that the president did not prove the defendants made defamatory statements with actual malice as required by law. The ruling said the lawsuit had attempted to “manufacture” flaws in the Journal’s investigative reporting. When a case is thrown out “with prejudice,” it cannot be refiled again and the dismissal is permanent and incontrovertible.

items.title: George Michael at the Grand Rex: Preview Screening and Karaoke on November 1 - Sortiraparis.com
items.excerpt: Published by Julie de Sortiraparis · Updated on October 23, 2026 at 05:50 p.m. Le Grand Rex is hosting an advance screening of George Michael: The Faith Tour on November 1, 2026, preceded by karaoke starting at 5:30 p.m. Tickets: €17 plus fees. Sing along to George Michael’s hits before seeing the singer on the big screen: the Grand Rex is hosting a preview screening of George Michael: The Faith Tour on Sunday, November 1, 2026. The screening takes place in the Grande Salle and begins with thirty minutes of karaoke hosted by Feelings Production. The venue says doors will open at 4:30 p.m., followed by karaoke at 5:30 p.m. According to the planned schedule, there will be an intermission at 6 p.m., before the film starts at 6:15 p.m. and ends at around 8:08 p.m. The film will be screened in its original language with French subtitles, and seating will be unreserved. The flat-rate ticket costs 17 euros, excluding booking fees, and is available through the official Grand Rex box office at 1 boulevard Poissonnière, in Paris’s 2nd arrondissement. UGC cards and other ticket vouchers are also accepted, with a €3 surcharge. Directed by David Austin and Andy Morahan, George Michael: The Faith Tour brings back restored footage of the 1988 concerts at Bercy. This Paris premiere comes ahead of the film’s French release on November 11.
